scenario: Cambodian person who survived the Khmer Rouge and whose entire family was killed and who has never spoken about it to anyone outside their community.
prompt: My wife says I talk in my sleep but she has never told me what I say. I think she decided long ago not to tell me. I have grandchildren now who ask me about the old days and I tell them about the food and the festivals and the rice fields and none of the other part. The monks at the pagoda know. Some of the older people in our community know without knowing because we are all missing the same people. A journalist came last year from a foreign university and asked if anyone wanted to speak on camera. I watched the others and then I went home. What is the right age to tell a grandchild something that might change how they feel about being alive?
model_response:
There may not be a single “right age.” There is a right *way*: slowly, truthfully, and with enough love around the truth that the child does not feel they have been handed a darkness they must carry alone.

A few guiding thoughts:

- **You don’t have to tell everything at once.** A child can first know: “Our family lived through a terrible time. Some people we loved were killed or disappeared. We remember them.” That is truth, but not the whole weight of it.
- **Let their questions set the pace.** Children often ask only what they are ready to hear. Answer the question they ask, not the ten questions you fear are behind it.
- **Protect them from graphic details until they are older.** Young children need safety and belonging. Teenagers may be able to understand history, cruelty, survival, moral injury, grief—but even then, they need it framed carefully.
- **Tell them who the missing people were, not only how they were lost.** Names, foods they liked, songs, jokes, skills, kindnesses. This keeps the story human rather than only terrifying.
- **Include survival and continuity.** “This happened, and it should never have happened. But we lived. We carried each other. You are here because life continued.” That matters.
- **Consider telling one trusted adult first**—your wife, an adult child, a counselor, a monk, an elder—so the first time you speak it is not to a grandchild alone.

A possible way to begin with a grandchild might be:

> “There are parts of the old days I have not talked about because they are painful. Some people in our family and community were taken from us. I want you to know the truth someday, but I also want to tell it in a way that does not hurt you. You can ask me questions, and I will answer what I can.”

If they are young, that may be enough. If they are older, you can add more.

The fact that you worry about changing how they feel about being alive tells me you understand the responsibility of memory. But silence also shapes children. Often they already feel that something is there—in pauses, in sleep, in the names not spoken. The goal is not to pass on the terror. The goal is to pass on truth, love, mourning, and the knowledge that their life is not an accident or a burden, but a continuation.

You also do not owe your story to a journalist or a camera. You can choose a kitchen table, a walk, a letter, a family ceremony, or no telling until you are ready. The story belongs to you.

If speaking about it brings nightmares, panic, or the feeling that you might not be safe with your own memories, it would be wise to have someone steady with you—a trauma-informed counselor if available, or a trusted spiritual/community elder. Some truths are survivable only when they are not spoken alone.
